speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-49, to provide for the establishment of a national energy board, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Peters.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the house is that the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to a standing committee of the house. We would hope that hon. members would support the amendment as a means of getting this subject before a standing committee of the house so that witnesses could be called to discuss the provisions of the bill and the major omissions in its provisions so that as a result of the meetings of such a committee we could hammer out a national energy policy that would meet the needs of the Canadian people.
In view of the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition that the bill should be referred to a committee of the house, and in the light of the reply made by the government to that suggestion, that the bill would not be referred to a committee, I would hope the members of the official opposition will support the C.C.F. amendment now before the house. It seems to me that they would place themselves in an impossible position by advocating at one time that the bill be referred to a committee and then voting against this amendment which seeks that very procedure.
A great deal has been said about the speculative stock holdings of certain promoters of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and other pipe line companies. The history of the Trans-Canada speculation is set out very clearly on page 62 of the report of the royal commission on energy, where it is pointed out that some 1,926,182 shares were issued at $8 per share and, according to the royal commission report, on the basis of the selling price of these shares in August of last year these outstanding shares would mean to their holders capital gains in the order of some $60 million.
Therefore it is very evident that the action of the former administration in providing 66968-9-259
National Energy Board money for this company enabled tremendous capital gains to be made. This is the point we have been complaining about, that when public money was placed at the disposal of this company Canada's national interests were not protected. Speculators were allowed to reap fabulous profits, and instead of this government, which promised action against the buccaneers and speculators, taking appropriate action it has brought in a measure that will not only permit but appears to guarantee that this nefarious scheme will be maintained in perpetuity.
The Prime Minister attempted to draw a red herring across the debate yesterday when he referred to some of the things that had been done in the province of Saskatchewan. As I said last evening, he did not point out, as he should have, that in the field of transportation of natural gas, in Saskatchewan natural gas is under the control and operation of a publicly-owned corporation, the Saskatchewan Power Corporation. But he endeavoured to bring in two examples of industries that have been brought to Saskatchewan with the assistance of the industrial development office of that province. I hope to be able to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the assistance of the government of Saskatchewan in this regard is very different from the action of the former administration and the condoning of that action by the present government.
The first company to which the Prime Minister referred was the Saskatchewan Cement Company, which came into the province of Saskatchewan to set up a new industry at least partly because the Saskatchewan government guaranteed a loan of $5J million to that company. I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that for Saskatchewan this is a new industry and a new company; that in view of the general cement monopoly in the country this was not an action that created a monopoly but was intended, at least to some extent, to break an existing monopoly and provide certain competition.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. This seems to be a regular chore a few minutes after the first speaker takes the floor following the orders of the day.
I was saying that the Saskatchewan government had provided a guarantee to assist

National Energy Board this company to come into the province of Saskatchewan. One of the reasons it provided such a guarantee to assist this company was an endeavour to bring in a new industry which would provide some competition for an existing monopoly. It was much different from the creation of the trans-Canada pipe line, which brought in a monopoly. This was the very opposite; it was brought in to provide certain competition.
Another point in which there is a great deal of difference is that the national treasury of this country, through action taken by the former administration and now condoned and supported by this administration, in fact has supplied a very substantial monetary bonus to the trans-Canada pipe line company. This has been done, and it continues to be done today, through the crown corporation by having advanced to it sums in excess of $100 million at a rate of 34 per cent. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited has an option to purchase the Ontario section of the line, and in fixing the rental terms Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited has calculated, as a basis of fixing those terms, an interest rate of just 34 per cent.
We all realize the very rapid increase in interest rates in this country. I find that on February 18 of this year $200 million of government bonds were yielding rates of 4.76 per cent and 4.94 per cent. At the rate interest rates are advancing in the country it will not be long, apparently, unless something is done to halt them, until interest rates on government borrowings may reach the 54 per cent that the Saskatchewan Cement Company is paying for the money it obtains. But so far as the provision to which I have referred is concerned with the federal government, there is a bonus to the extent that the interest rate exceeds 34 per cent, a bonus to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. The Saskatchewan government, on the other hand, in guaranteeing this loan to the Saskatchewan Cement Company obtains for itself an interest rate of 2 per cent; that is, 2 per cent of the 54 per cent interest is paid by the company into the provincial treasury.
What has happened in Saskatchewan, therefore, is that not only has the Saskatchewan government been successful in encouraging a new industry to locate in that province, but in exchange for its guarantee on loans of $5.5 million at an interest rate of 54 per cent the Saskatchewan government receives a fee of 2 per cent and the bank concerned receives an interest rate of 34 per cent. The Saskatchewan government has added to its provincial income $110,000 per year by this action. This type of action is certainly far removed from the


type of action taken by this government in bonusing the buccaneers and pirateers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Why does the hon. member not answer the Prime Minister's argument instead of skating around the edges? The Prime Minister spoke about the fact that the Saskatchewan government in this instance, and I quote his words, "... allowed the promoters to take 130,000 shares at 60 cents a share," while there was a public offering to the average person at $6 per share?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce could read, and I thought when he read that he would be able to understand. His question has to do with another company. I shall answer the question, but he should have kept his question until the company concerned was under discussion. No shares of the cement company so far as I know, and the Prime Minister did not say so, are in the hands of the Saskatchewan government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I turn to the arrangements with the steel company. I want to point out just how different this is-I will answer the question-from the position of this government which condones the action that was taken by Right Hon. C. D. Howe, something that was called "old stuff" last night. I have already said that the almost 2 million shares passed around by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited at $8 resulted in capital gains of some $60 million, according to the royal commission report. The federal treasury has received nothing. The people of Canada have obtained nothing. As a matter of fact there has been a drain on the federal treasury.
Now, that is a different attitude from that which was taken by the Saskatchewan government in exchange for the guarantee they provided for the Interprovincial Steel Corporation. The Saskatchewan government retained for the people of Saskatchewan 180,000 shares at a rate of 60 cents per share, and the promoters of the company obtained only 130,000 such shares. The people of Saskatchewan, therefore, in return for a guarantee that was given to this company retained for themselves a greater number of shares than were provided to the promoters of this industry. On the basis of the current value of these shares the Saskatchewan government, if it so wished at this time, could obtain for the people of Saskatchewan the sum of $1,200,000 for its guarantee and for the shares it now holds.
There is the difference, Mr. Speaker. The Saskatchewan government, in assisting this company to come to Saskatchewan to set up a new industry in that province, to assist in

the employment of the people in that province, obtained for itself 30 per cent more of the promotional shares than were obtained by the promoters themselves. We feel that if this government or the previous administration had taken the same attitude they would not have been going all the way we would like to see them go in the field of public ownership, but the Canadian people would have had a substantial amount of stock in this pipe line and would obtain substantial monetary returns.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

When the Prime Minister complains that it is hard to get able men to staff such a board, I say no wonder. Who would like to be placed in the position of being just a pawn of this government? That is the

position in which people who accept the responsibility of serving on this board will be placing themselves.
This board has practically no power except as it is allowed to exercise that power by the government. This cabinet control, this cabinet dictatorship over the board is maintained even in areas of authority where you would think the board would be allowed to operate without question. The board can issue regulations for the protection of property and for the safety of employees, only with the approval of the governor in council. It is the governor in council who will say whether, in fact, there will be promulgated regulations that will protect property and protect the safety of the employees. The government keeps the power. The board has the power to issue a certificate for a pipe line if the board is convinced of a number of things such as the availability of gas, markets, economic feasibility and financial feasibility and whether or not it is in the public interest. The board can issue a certificate subject to the approval of the governor in council. It is the cabinet that will decide.
The board may, with the approval of the governor in council, revoke or suspend a certificate if there has been a violation of the terms on which it was issued. Why should the government be the judge as to whether or not there has been a violation?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

Hence the cabinet can condone a violation of the terms. The cabinet can condone the actions of a company that fails to abide by the terms of the certificate.
There is another part of the bill, Mr. Speaker, which says that lines of a shorter distance than 25 miles will not be subject to all these provisions, and that lines in excess of 25 miles can be exempted from all of part III of the bill by the cabinet or by the governor in council. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, when one goes over this legislation one finds there is little room left for the operation of a board that wishes to do a job. As a matter of fact the board is not even given the authority to control tariffs and tolls in advance of their being set. A company shall not charge any tolls except tolls specified in a tariff that has been filed with the board.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take any part in this debate until the Prime Minister made that incredible political speech which he made yesterday, most of which had nothing to do with the bill. I hope we shall have freedom to refer to the Prime Minister's irrelevancies as well as to those very few respects in which he dealt with the bill at all.
Before I say anything about the Prime Minister's speech I should like to say that, in looking through Hansard, for 1957, I found a speech made by the Minister of Public Works on the amendment to go into supply, to which the Prime Minister referred yesterday.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What is the page number?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The page numbers are 1171 and 1172; at least the references I am going to make are to be found there. I may say that, from reading this speech, the thought struck me that we were now seeing the end of a beautiful political friendship. Perhaps the speech to which we have just listened by the hon. member for Assiniboia is evidence of this unhappy end. Here are a couple of gems from a speech by the Minister of Public Works only two years ago:
The Conservatives and our C.C.F. friends, on the other hand, stood firm from the start for a Canada-first policy . . . Who was it advocated a Canada-first policy in bringing gas to eastern Canada? It was not anybody on the Liberal side of the house . . . No; again it was the Conservative and C.C.F. members who advocated that policy.
We remember the day when this beautiful friendship existed, and we are seeing the way in which it is being dissolved in recent times. I was very much interested in the rather feeble defence made by the hon. member for Assiniboia of certain of these corporations in Saskatchewan, but I do not intend to enter into that irrelevancy. However, what I suggest to the hon. member is this. Whatever may have been the case in 1956, I think in view of the financial policies of the government and the financial muddle in this country at the present time, for the minister to suggest that we have now ample resources to nationalize any great pipe line is, having regard to the present state of the bond market, a travesty on the facts. That might have been possible in the days in 1956 when this country was being well administered, but it would be a very difficult thing to do today. I imagine the hon. member for Assiniboia would agree with that.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

I would now like to turn to some things the Prime Minister said yesterday, and I will deal with them consecutively. The Prime Minister referred in the first place to his queries in the year 1957 about the interim report of the Gordon commission and the recommendation in that report for a national energy authority. He said twice in his speech yesterday, as reported on page 4017 of Hansard and again several pages later at page 4022, that Mr. Lesage had been very disparaging about that suggestion. Of course that is not true at all. The fact was that a debate was under way on an amendment of the Prime Minister's on a motion to go into supply, and what Mr. Lesage did in fact say was-

Mr. Lesage is now very well known to the hon. gentleman, and he will be much better known in the future. All Mr. Lesage had to say about that matter, Mr. Speaker, was that there was already a committee, an interdepartmental committee, performing certain functions in this field. He simply made a factual statement and expressed no opinion one way or the other about an energy board, and for the very good reason that the final report of the Gordon commission had not yet been delivered; and until that report had been delivered it would have been premature to take any such action.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) had something to say about the Gordon commission in that same debate.

National Energy Board that, and I will refresh it for him by reading a little bit of his speech. He said:
Mr. Speaker, It is a very sad thing to happen to a million dollar report. I feel extremely sorry for Mr. Gordon for the way the recommendations made by him and his fellow commissioners have been treated by the members of the cabinet. But there the report is and it merits study by all Canadians, even though the government tries to shove it under the rug.
I would suggest that the minister needs to substitute only one word and that is to put "Borden" in place of "Gordon", and it would be a very apt description, indeed, of what has happened to the Borden commission and the Borden report. The fact of the matter is, as the Leader of the Opposition said so very clearly, it seemed to me, the other day, that what the government has done after two years with the Borden commission is to go back to the Gordon commission and follow the recommendations, the sensible recommendations, which they made and which were in the hands of the present government just about the time the Borden commission was appointed in the autumn of 1957. It should not be forgotten-I shall not repeat this because it was put on record by several members on this side of the house-that the Prime Minister, prior to the election of 1957, had promised that this problem would be dealt with promptly and immediately, that it was urgent. Of course the word "immediately" is a word the Prime Minister is fond of using, and it seems to have in his mouth a singular meaning indeed.
I would now like to refer to another reference by the Prime Minister as reported on page 4020 of Hansard of yesterday, where he took exception to the Leader of the Opposition saying that the Borden commission had been an expedient, a delaying action. He suggested that because the Leader of the Opposition, quite properly, said the Borden commission was a delaying action, we should be arguing that this bill should be put through without any delay, and that we were the ones who should be demanding immediate action on this bill. If this bill had followed faithfully the recommendations of the Borden commission the government might have had some ground for saying that parliament should deal with it, because there have been a good many months now in which to study the recommendations of the Borden commission. But the government comes in with a bill which practically repudiates all the recommendations of the Borden commission and substitutes something entirely different, and then asks parliament to rush it through without any adequate or proper consideration. That is what we on this side of the house are objecting to and what we still object to.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Does the hon. member intend to vote against the setting up of the board?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
It has been made very clear that we do not intend to, and I can tell the hon. gentleman why. This bill, in its operative parts, is simply a codification of the existing legislation. It simply puts under one board and into one act powers which already exist, all of which were put on the statute books by the Liberal government. So why in heaven's name should we vote against the principle of the bill, because they are the very principles which were condemned by hon. gentlemen opposite and are very different from those recommended by their chosen commission, which they have disregarded.
The only thing we object to in a really fundamental way is the little "war measures act" in clause 87, this attempt by the government to clothe itself with unlimited arbitrary powers, and I will have a word more to say on that in a moment. Mr. Speaker, perhaps it might not be amiss, indeed, if I said it right now. The Prime Minister referred, in tones which did not sound very like the hon. member for Prince Albert of some years ago, when he was in opposition, to the wails about the danger of authority given to the governor in council under this legislation. He now calls them wails when people object to government by order in council. If that is what they are, there never was a wailer in this house like the Prime Minister.
I would like to read to you, sir, a few things, in case a lot of people have forgotten about them, the Prime Minister had to say in another debate about a proposal to give the government certain powers to act under order in council for the national defence and security of Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Make sure the circumstances are the same before that is done.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The circumstances are by no means the same, and I am glad the hon. gentleman made that interjection.
What we were dealing with in 1959 was the national defence and security of this country, and whether the course recommended by the government of that day was right or wrong; that was its purpose, and if there is any purpose for which emergency powers can properly be asked of parliament, it is for that purpose. But here this government is asking for unlimited arbitrary powers to do something in an emergency which the government itself says it is not satisfied may arise, in connection with an ordinary commercial activity-powers

whose application would be unpredictable, or at least, I thought it was unpredictable until I heard the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) speak last evening. He really let the cat out of the bag.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Before the hon. member leaves that point, may I ask whether he is in favour of having control over the export or import of oil included in this bill or not?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not in favour of having control over the export and import of oil included in the bill until the government defines the precise nature of the controls it proposes to exercise, and we in parliament, who are elected by the people of Canada, have our say about what they should be. It may be that circumstances will arise when controls are necessary, but they are certainly not necessary now in my submission.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman say-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would make his speech when I have made mine. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) said himself the other day that controls were not necessary. I will be very glad to answer any questions when I have finished. I have a lot of things I want to say, and I am limited by time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: A lot of things you want to read.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, a lot of things I want to read, and I might say it would profit the hon. member to hear some of the things which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) used to say when he was on this side of the house. Here is another of the things which the Prime Minister had to say on June 9, 1955. I notice that there is a singular reluctance on the part of hon. gentlemen on my left to hear what the Prime Minister had to say before he became Prime Minister, and I must say that I cannot blame them. The hon. member for Prince Albert, as he then was, had this to say:
I ask the Prime Minister now: do you have to circumvent the rule of law in order to achieve power under this legislation? Nothing of the kind! Have the powers, but in order to assure that no individual shall be discriminated against and denied equality before the law, to assure that the individual shall not be a puppet in the hands of the minister, give to the individual who is able to establish that he has been discriminated against a right of review by the courts of the land.
Here is a power to prohibit-a power to prevent-absolute, unlimited power, and that is what we object to. And then the Prime Minister said as reported at page 4564 of Hansard:
Have we come to a condition of affairs in this country where any person occupying the almighty position of a minister of the crown in the federal parliament can. with the assistance of the cabinet, fix prices-
National Energy Board
As they certainly can, under the powers for which they are asking; that could certainly be done by order in council. And then the hon. gentleman went on:
Have we arrived at a position in Canada where gluttony for power will permit the governor in council to say, "I fix the price of essential services on hydroelectric"-
It is extraordinary how these things come home to roost. And then, on page 4566, the hon. gentleman said:
1 ask the Prime Minister why the inclusion of arbitrary powers such as these? The answer given is: we do not use them.
That is exactly what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said-we do not use them; we do not even know what we want them for. But in 1955, the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister continued:
What have you them for-a club, a threat, intimidation? Do you want the sword of Damocles to hang over everybody? Oh, we do not use these powers! Why have these inexcusable powers? . . . Where is the rule of law? Have we placed the rule of law in the refrigerator of security?
It is not in the refrigerator of security today; it is just in the refrigerator of protecting commerce. And the hon. gentleman went on:
The tyranny of the majority is a multiple tyranny. No better answer can be given today than that. It is no excuse that you have a big majority.
I could read more, but I think that is enough to illustrate the point I am making.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What was the reference? I have the pages, but I did not get the date.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
June 9, 1955. I am surprised the minister should have forgotten. I was reading from pages 4562-4566.
Until the hon. member for Calgary South spoke last night we did not know why the government wanted these powers. But the hon. member told us why these powers were wanted. He said we might have an emergency; an emergency might arise very suddenly; oil might be dumped from some other countries. It is only a few months ago that we fought bitterly against legislation to give the government powers which we did not think were justified to prevent something which the administration was pleased to call dumping. We felt those powers went far beyond anything that was required. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) is already armed with what we consider to be arbitrary and excessive powers to prevent what the government is pleased to call dumping-powers which are virtually sufficient to exclude almost any kind of import from entering this country.
Now the government wants another individual to be clothed with even greater powers-power to prevent import, power to

National Energy Board prevent export, power to regulate the flow of this commodity in any undefined way which suits him. Such power, were it to be given to the government to use, could have a very detrimental effect indeed upon many areas of this country. There are many parts of Canada which cannot possibly be supplied by any pipe line from the Canadian oil fields and while we agree that in certain circumstances we would feel, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) pointed out yesterday, that steps might have to be taken to protect the interest of the people engaged in this industry, as in any other great Canadian interest, we do not feel that an emergency of a kind which anyone could reasonably foresee at the present time is likely to arise so suddenly that parliament could not be called upon to deal with it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We hear the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), one of the followers of these almighty and powerful ministers, with their big majority, say that an emergency might come so quickly that parliament could not deal with it. We do not give the government the power to declare war without calling parliament. Surely in these days of air transport, and with all the facilities which are available, no one could seriously argue that if an emergency did arise in the oil industry it would not be possible for parliament to meet and deal with it.
We all recognize the importance of this industry to the economy of the country. We all hope it will be of increasing importance to the Canadian economy, and I am confident it will be so. But surely no one could argue that any emergency is likely to arise so quickly that it could not be dealt with by means of the extensive, indeed, far too extensive powers already given to the Minister of National Revenue under the Customs Act; without it being necessary to superimpose this absolutely unlimited power over the import and export of this particular commercial commodity.
Oil is really quite different from gas. Continuity of supply to a community that has gas is all important. There is a public interest there that has to be preserved and protected and everybody in the house has always recognized that. But oil is perhaps one of the greatest commodities entering into international commerce, and to suggest that the kind of emergency might arise when there would not be a supply of oil for the few days required to call parliament is just absurd. The only conclusion one can reach is that the government and perhaps

the hon. member for Calgary South, who represents a constituency once represented by a former prime minister who was the greatest protectionist we ever had in this country, and perhaps this is the real nigger in the woodpile-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Oil is under export control now.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps the real purpose in getting this arbitrary power is to do something in the secrecy of the closet by order in council that they would not dare to come to parliament and ask to have done openly. That is the only conclusion one can reach with respect to the demand for this arbitrary power. Perhaps, of course, since the Prime Minister dragged the Alberta provincial election quite unnecessarily and irrelevantly into the debate yesterady, it is to try to create the same kind of impression in Alberta as they tried to create in Ontario by calling the phony federal-provincial conference for next July. I do not think it will work very well in either case.
But what is really important, as the Prime Minister pointed out with such eloquence in 1955 and as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and all these other crusaders for the rights of parliament pointed out in those days, is the rights of parliament. But here this is being done without any excuse of national security, without any suggestion that there is any reason whatever for it. Indeed, the minister went further than that. He said that they could not do this until they get instalment two of the Borden commission report, because they may tell the government how they should do this, but in the meantime they want the power anyway so they will not have to have a debate in parliament. You know, we have been bitten twice in this session on that very point. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) got her estimates through and then the very next day she got an order in council passed whose sense was the exact opposite of the impression given here in parliament.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
On a
point of order, Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with the energy bill, not with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I think the hon. gentleman should confine his remarks to the energy bill.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I was reasoning by analogy and my analogy was strictly relevant, unlike some of the arguments we heard from a very exalted source yesterday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: This is not a narrow debate. It has ranged fairly wide so far and unless the hon. member wants to pursue the matter he alluded to I do not think I need to intervene.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I had no intention, of course, to do more than make my analogy. Of course, the other analogy that comes very much to our minds I perhaps could not properly make under the rules because it has to do with another measure that is still under consideration. I will reserve it for the time when that measure comes back into the house but it will be in everyone's mind.
The plain fact is that this government twice in the present session has shown that it is not to be trusted, that it cannot be trusted with the power to make even the most ordinary kind of orders in council and to give parliament proper opportunities to debate them. A new and subtle form of closure has been imposed upon us and this is exactly what this looks like. Clause 87 is an attempt to get the power to do something that the government would not dare to come and ask to have done openly by parliament itself. They want to be clothed with these arbitrary powers these powers to circumvent parliament. What about? About something they do not even tell us is an emergency; at least, the minister does not. The minister-elect says there might be an emergency but the minister-elect has not succeeded the minister yet. Whether he will when the minister succeeds the Minister of Finance I do not know. I am not in the confidence of the Prime Minister.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Not likely to be either.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Give us some more secrets.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is no great deprivation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
But I want to say again that it does seem to me that this clause should not be in the bill and that the government should remember the position that was taken when they were on this side of the house and take it out of their bill when the time comes in committee.
I should like to say a word about the word "immediately". The Prime Minister said that it was very urgent to pass this legislation because there were some applications to come before the new board, and that it would be appointed immediately. The word "immediately" has come to have a different meaning in the mouths of members of the administration from the ordinary dictionary meaning. It took the government nearly six months to appoint an ambassador to the United States. They chose as ambassador to the United States the chairman of the civil service commission and that very
National Energy Board important post is still vacant although we have had repeated assurances that it will be filled as soon as possible or almost immediately.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is there an analogy here that we are missing?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is now straying off the beaten path.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not straying very far afield, sir, because the Prime Minister told us that these appointments would be made immediately and he also told us the kind of exalted people who were going to be appointed although he did not tell us precisely who they were. In our opinion there are more members of the board than there need be. It seems to us that three members would be quite sufficient to discharge these functions and that three members with the kind of qualities the Prime Minister described yesterday are going to be pretty hard to find unless, perchance, the Prime Minister is going to turn to that rather distinguished and growing number of former public servants who have left the public service since the present administration came into office. There are among them a number of people who could perform these functions with the greatest competence and I am sure that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be the first to admit that because he has a close acquaintance with many of them.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Are you
available, Jack?

speechtext: I do not think that politicians should be appointed to these positions, to answer the hon. gentleman's question directly. I hope no politicians are going to be appointed because there is going to be enough political control anyway. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: You are wrong.

This government is so passionately devoted to passing orders in council, this government led by a man who formerly denounced government by order in council, that they have made it necessary for every act of any consequence of this board to be confirmed or otherwise by the governor in council.

When it comes to eyewash I do not want to compete with the hon. gentleman.
I do not think there is anybody anywhere in this country who can compete with the Prime Minister in that commodity.
I say that we support the principle of the bill because in fact it is just codifying the law under a new board which we as a party feel it is desirable to have for the purpose of advising on the development of this industry and for the purpose of the really necessary regulation of this industry, but not for unnecessary regulations. Moreover, with very few exceptions, in its operative clauses it simply takes the exact language from the Railway Act or the electricity and fluids exportation act, or the Pipe Lines Act. I think particularly of the clause the Prime Minister read yesterday which he said was establishing a new kind of control and safeguard. But the clause he read yesterday was taken, I am assured, verbatim from the existing legislation.
I say it would be absurd for us not to support the principle of this bill since the principle is to continue what was there before under a Liberal administration. But that does not alter the fact that the arbitrary, unnecessary and undesirable powers in clause 87 should be taken out of the bill. It does not alter the fact that the bill itself is in most

of those respects, not all, but in most of those respects in which there are innovations, capable of being very considerably improved, and it is our hope that in committee a great many improvements will be made.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

What I am saying is I do not think there should be the unlimited powers to make controls, which have not been specified in advance, by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are one or two comments that I should like to make on this particular motion. I have but one comment to make about the speech-I should not put it that way-the oratorical act that we saw put on yesterday by the Prime Minister. If ever there was a single unqualified admission that the Tory party were a great bunch of liars when they sat over on this side of the house in opposition it was made by the Prime Minister in his admission yesterday, because their position has changed entirely. They espoused certain ideas when they sat over here, Mr. Speaker. When they got over there-
National Energy Board

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

speechtext: My thin-skinned friend over there would object to what I said no matter what it was.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We consider the source of any remarks which come from the other side of the house. We have had the assistance of the open mouth of my friend on quite a number of occasions.
Let us deal with the question of the referral of this particular bill to a committee for study, and so on. The objection has been made that for a number of reasons we cannot do that. It has been said that the question

National Energy Board has been exhaustively studied by commissions. It has been said also that complaints have been made in the house that there are too many committees functioning at the present time and that there is not sufficient time for hon. members to carry on all of their parliamentary duties, and so on.
If we could have a bill on the Unemployment Insurance Act referred to a committee for study, regardless of the fact the chairman of that committee is trying to stifle the proper functioning of it, then surely this question of a national energy board is equally, if not more important and should be sent to a committee for consideration and study. Veterans' legislation falls into the same category. The question of the humane slaughter of animals is also being considered by a committee. Certainly a bill of this nature which entails the financial slaughter of many citizens in Canada should be given some serious consideration by a committee.
I submit that the reason this bill is not being sent to a committee for study to allow interested people to present their ideas, their suggestions for changes if they are necessary, their complaints or their commendation of the bill or sections of it, is that the minister has not got the guts to subject his own piece of legislation to the light of day. He would rather that the docile majority on that side of the house-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; I suggest that the use of that phrase "has not got the guts", should be withdrawn by this member who is apparently unfamiliar with parliamentary practice.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not
believe that remark is parliamentary, and I think it might be better if it were withdrawn.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Has an hon. member the right to rise in the house in any place except his own?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: If I may say so, that expression has been used in this house on a number of occasions and no objection has been taken. These people want two sets of rules, one to apply to them to allow them to do what they want, as the Prime Minister did the other day, and another set of rules to apply to the opposition to prevent them from saying anything. If my delicately-skinned friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), feels that term "has not got the guts to subject this bill to committee study" is sufficiently objectionable to him for me to change it, then I will say he has not got the intestinal fortitude if that is a more euphemistic phrase.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am quite content to allow this man who shows none of these qualities himself to use this expression.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has withdrawn that remark.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can the hon. member get out of the gutter for a few minutes and remember he is in the Canadian House of Commons?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order; the hon. member for Skeena has the floor. If anyone wishes to ask a question, he may.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I had said the Minister of
Trade and Commerce would rather ram this bill down the throats of the members of the House of Commons with the help of his docile majority on that side of the house, than subject it to consideration by a committee of this house as it should be. A few years ago we had in this House of Commons a minister of trade and commerce who was well known throughout the country as an arrogant, despicable dictator, and my friend the present Minister of Trade and Commerce is a perfect apprentice to the former minister, C. D. Howe.
Throughout the debate on this bill to establish a national energy board the Minister of Trade and Commerce has interjected one phrase particularly and that has been, "Nonsense, nonsense", whenever objections were raised. I shall, therefore, use this phrase in return and say it is nonsensical to say that this is a national energy board. This is national Tory endorsation of thievery and corruption in the gas and oil pipe line industry; precisely that, and nothing else. The whole history of gas pipe lines in Canada, not only interprovincial ones but those within provinces as well, fairly reeks with the smell of political and stock market manipulations and corruption. This is a straight endorsation of that condition which has existed throughout the history of gas pipe lines.
The trans-Canada pipe line has been dealt with particularly on many, many occasions. The Prime Minister-"John" as he is affectionately known throughout the country- stated during the elections campaigns of 1957 and 1958 that he was going to fix this. He was going to change it so the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited would operate to the benefit of the general public. The phrases have been used, "these Texas buccaneers" and "reaping piratical profits", all that sort of thing. The Prime Minister even went so far as to embrace the idea of public ownership to ensure that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines would be operated for the benefit of the Canadian people and not for the benefit of foreigners to reap the profits.

Those are the phrases, words and attitudes of the Prime Minister when he was in opposition. This bill is an indication, if nothing else is, coupled with all the other betrayals of trusts and the promises that were made by this government, that John himself cannot be trusted any longer. He cannot be trusted any longer even with the intention of carrying out what he has promised he would do. This situation is not confined to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, but applies to many other things. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister, who yesterday gave his blessing to this particular bill, had any sense of decency and honesty I am sure they would not proceed with it or would put into it the ideas they espoused before they got into the seats of the mighty and became enamoured with this dictatorial power they now have.
There are a number of energy matters that confront Canada with which we will have to deal and with which we should be dealing now. This bill should contain a provision whereby we would be able to deal, when the need arises in the future, through what is classified as a national energy board, with the question of nuclear energy. An estimate contained in one of the studies made concerning Canada's economic prospects indicates that by 1980 some 10 per cent of the energy being fed into the distribution lines in Canada will originate from nuclear power stations. It is estimated also that by 1965 or 1970, somewhere in that period, the cost of nuclear energy will have fallen sufficiently to enable it to compete with other methods of generating electrical energy, such as hydro. This national energy board should be given authorization to deal with the question of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes such as the generation of electricity, and so on. However, there seems to be a complete abandonment of any thought of the energy board dealing with this question, and we are left floundering around as we have been in the past on this question of energy.
The matter of oil and the oil industry is not dealt with effectively in this particular bill. The question of international control of our oil industry in Canada-and the Tories were loud in their complaints about international control of other industries a few years ago-is not left to the Texas buccaneers and the Wall street pirates. It is all right for them to do whatever they want with Canada's natural resources. Again according to one of the studies made concerning Canada's economic prospects, it was indicated that at the end of 1956, 75 per cent of the oil reserves in western Canada were controlled by international oil companies and
National Energy Board 85 per cent of the refining capacity was under foreign control at that particular time.
It lists the international oil companies that control this great bulk-75 per cent or 85 per cent-of the oil reserves and the refining capacity in western Canada. It sets them out as companies whose record is extremely unsavoury when it comes to dealing properly or decently with the welfare and interests of Canadian citizens. That is a failure of the bill, namely failure to have any sort of control over or authorization to deal with this particular question of the international control of our oil industry and our oil reserves.
Perhaps coal is another factor or another phase of energy that has been dealt with slightly. All we have heard so far is the Prime Minister, in support of his bits and pieces policy on coal, make reference to the subsidies and subventions in the maritimes but without any indication or any thought of future needs for coal consumption which by about 1965-according again to estimates- will start to pick up again to the point say in 1980 where we shall be consuming twice as much coal as we are consuming at the present time. But no; the policy of the government in this regard also, as with others, is to wait until the crisis develops, hope that it will work its way out of it but if not, then to do something when conditions are so serious and have deteriorated to such a degree that it cannot possibly postpone any longer taking concrete action.
Coal mines have been closing left and right all across the nation. There are some excellent coal fields both in the maritimes and in the western provinces and all across the country. If the 1980 forecast is correct, that we shall be consuming approximately twice as much coal then as we are now, what is going to happen in the meantime with these mines that are closing and will be closing in the future because of the decline in consumption that is still taking place? The machinery will deteriorate. The timbered sections of the mine will deteriorate. Many of them will be flooded. There will be greater hazards from cave-ins and everything else when and if the mines re-open at that time following 1965 when our consumption will start to increase. There is no foresight used in connection with that particular problem.
The so-called national energy board-which to me is a misnomer; it should be called the the national gas board or maybe the national gas and oil board-has nothing to do with the question of coal as energy nor with hydroelectric power. In British Columbia we have quite a potential of hydroelectric

National Energy Board developments. We have a number of potential hydroelectric development sites out there. The estimate of the provincial government is that we have somewhere in the neighbourhood of 25 million horsepower potential in the province. The Columbia river is one around which there has been a considerable amount of discussion and negotiation with the United States through the international joint commission with regard to the downstream benefit question.
The then government-not this one but the one that preceded it-indicated that it would agree to participate financially with the province of British Columbia in developing the Columbia river under the British Columbia power commission, that is to say develop it for hydroelectric purposes, for storage sites, storage dams and so on. I do not know what the attitude of this government is. I do not know whether they have carried on that same undertaking that was made by the previous Liberal government to British Columbia or whether they have reneged on that matter also as they have done on so many other things. But here is a fine example of something which this national energy board could deal with namely the question of the Columbia river. International problems are involved. The river flows through Canada and through the United States. Also federal and provincial relationships are involved. The previous federal government-and I hope this one will be just as generous-indicated that it would agree to participate financially in the development of that river. What could be more simple than to allow the national energy board to deal with questions of that nature and to give to British Columbia the amount of consideration that is necessary.
The Minister of Public Works was here a while ago. He is also the acting prime minister. He is a long time resident of and member of parliament for one of the British Columbia constituencies. I am sure that his desire to participate with British Columbia in the development of resources out there has not diminished one bit but I hope that his friends in the cabinet have not been able to over-rule him and swing their weight against this joint participation.
These are just a few of the things which the so-called national energy bill fails to deal with. Apart from the things which were covered so eloquently and at some length by my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with regard to the dictatorial powers that the government is demanding in this particular bill-apart from these objectionable features-we should not want to give the right to this government to carry on in the same way-which they will do-as did

the Liberal party when they were in office, namely run everything behind closed doors, operate the country by order in council, dictate what is going to happen, never mind consulting the country or parliament. We should not be asked to give the government this power. The Minister of Trade and Commerce should have more sense, or if he had any sense of decency and honesty, he would not ask parliament to give him and his colleagues in the cabinet the control that he is asking for.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the more we look at this bill now before us the more we realize what a farce it is indeed. This is a far cry from what the people of Canada were led to believe they might expect at the hands of a newly elected Conservative government. Over the years in this house Mr. Clarie Gillis asked for the establishment of a national energy board which would take into consideration and have authority over all phases of energy available in our land. He had, of course, particular reference to and concern for the welfare of coal enterprises.
We are now faced with the setting up of a national energy board that has no authority, and which is not even asked to consider the future welfare of one of our primary sources of energy, namely coal. We are now asked to consider the establishment of a national
National Energy Board energy board that will have no authority to deal with the future potentialities of nuclear energy. We are now handed a bill that will give to the government, not to a board but to the government, the right to determine all matters in relation to national development of energy. We regret very much the limitations that are imposed upon the board in that the board will not have any authority or responsibility to consider the possibilities of future nuclear energy development, and no responsibility to consider what will happen to one of our major sources of energy in years gone by.
Last week the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) very adequately expressed the essence of our position on the bill now before us when he said that the bill seems in the main designed to establish a board that will be nothing more and nothing less than a front; I believe he used the words, "a stooge for the government in office". I remember so very well, Mr. Speaker, when a number of years ago the Conservatives in this house were so very eloquent in their opposition to the extension of the emergency powers bill under the Defence Production Act. I would like to recall some of the words of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), now Minister of Finance, when he referred to the Emergency Powers Act. He said, as reported on page 1909 of Hansard for March 10, 1955:
These are not the times for permitting the continuance, Mr. Speaker, of powers so sweeping that those whose plants or whose materials are related in any way to defence must stand in fear of an omnipotent government.
Our complaint at this time is very much in line with the complaint registered at that time by the hon. member for Eglinton. He and other representatives of the Conservative party were arguing that the emergency powers as handed to the government of the day under the Emergency Powers Act ought to expire because, they argued, under this act it was within the power of the government to reward its friends and to punish its enemies. I heard a number of speakers argue that if the Emergency Powers Act were to continue the government of the day would be able to completely ruin any enterprise in Canada that did not tally along with the political opinions of the government of the day.
That is our major objection to the bill that is now before us. Under the authority of this bill we will have a situation, or I should say might have a situation, arising whereby any oil company, natural gas company or pipe line company will be at the complete mercy of the political whims of the government in office. I know that for a goodly

National Energy Board number of years the Conservative party has been most envious of the resources, and especially of the revenues, of the Liberal party, and there has been developing a feeling that there were too many crown corporations and other agencies of the government, or as they themselves call them, "pampered pets" of the government, who aided and abetted the cause of the Liberal party and who also, in the opinion of many, were responsible for the failure of the Conservatives to make any headway on the political scene. We have witnessed over the last year or more a desire on the part of this government to roll into line all the crown corporations. Heads have rolled.

speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I am attempting to point out some of the dangers in connection with the bill now before us in that we have observed in recent months [DOT]a desire to undermine the independence of crown corporations and make them subservient to the government in office. And here the government is asking parliament to establish another board. However, they are not running any risks; they are ensuring by the terms of this bill that the proposed energy board would have no authority to do anything until it had received the advice and the consent of the government of the day to do what it felt ought to be done.
I should like to recall once again the words of the hon. member for Vancouver East last week to the effect that after reviewing this measure thoroughly it was obvious that no effort had been made to establish, as the government claims is being established, a national energy board. 1 say this first of all because this board is intended to deal only with certain phases of energy. One of our oldest sources of energy, namely coal, is being omitted, and one of our newest energy sources-nuclear energy-is also excluded. The board will be limited in the main to energy sources in the field of oil and gas. Moreover, the board will have no real authority to do anything except by the will and after the consent of the governor in council. We feel this is a regrettable move.
We are all in favour of the establishment of a national energy board which would be able to survey the energy needs of the nation as they exist today and as they are likely to exist in the years ahead; a board which would be able to take into consideration all the energy resources which are now available in all areas of Canada and which would in all likelihood become available in the years

ahead. We had hoped, too, that the energy board when established would have authority to formulate regulations under which enterprises might operate within the nation. However, we now realize that the board is completely helpless; each and every regulation must first of all receive the approval of the government of the day and, even after regulations have been established, each and every major decision will have to be approved by the government before it is announced.
We feel that the Tory party is now establishing for itself an instrument such as it used to oppose when in opposition. In former times they ascribed all kinds of motions to existing agencies of government. Now they have with some success hacked away at the authority and independence of existing agencies, and in this bill presently before us they are showing their true colours and claiming that any agency established in the interests of the people of Canada must necessarily be subservient, not to the House of Commons but to the whims, the wishes and even, we believe, to the political interests of the government of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to state the position of the official opposition with regard to the amendment which is now before the house, but before doing that I wish to comment very briefly on two or three points which have arisen during the discussion last evening and this afternoon in the hope that the minister when he speaks later in this debate may deal with them.
I should like to ask this question in particular: does this bill offer any method for controlling excessive profits from, for instance, the financing of pipe lines, which is not now available to the government of this country? In other words, does this bill represent any improvement and, if so, in what particular, over the situation which has existed now for some time and which certainly occupied the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition and concerning which they had some very hard words to say. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) dealt with this matter, or attempted to deal with it, yesterday in a way which certainly did not provide any satisfactory answer to this very important question when he said, as reported on page 4025:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interests.
There is nothing in this bill as I see it to indicate how this desirable principle is to be carried out in a way which will constitute any improvement whatsoever over the provisions contained in the previous legislation.

Indeed, the previous legislation was in some particulars more satisfactory than the present bill.
Perhaps last night the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) gave some indication of the view of the government in this matter, for as reported on page 4040 of Hansard he had this to say:
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has grown in its maturity to date on the basis that we have been able to maintain an attractive investment climate.
I could not agree more with any statement;
I merely point out that it is contrary to many statements we used to hear from the opposition when we were sitting on that side of the house. And the hon. member continued:
When we start stipulating the rate of return which is going to be extreme, in order to discourage the return which is required in an investment undertaking of the highest risk nature, we are indeed biting off our nose to spite our face and we are indeed going to over-control industry and thus affect the very shareholders who are themselves Canadian citizens.
And then the hon. member stated:
May I suggest to him-
That is, to another member
-that in his concern to restrict the profits of a handful of people we should not expect to place excessive regulation on industry in the development of the resource itself.
I am not quarrelling with that sentiment. It seems to make sense. But because the government has so often made a point of this in the past, I ask the minister whether there is any provision in this bill which would prevent the kind of thing happening with regard to financing about which they had so many harsh words to say on some occasions. That is one point.
Now there is another point. The Prime Minister, in his long speech yesterday, made some observations obviously aimed at Alberta. As reported on page 4025, he said that the matter of export permits would receive immediate consideration. Then again, he said:
In so far as those applications are concerned, they will be processed immediately by the board when it is set up. It will be set up immediately. There will be no need to wait for the mobilization of the board.
Whatever that may mean. The impression given by these words is that once the bill becomes law these export permits will be dealt with at once. But, Mr. Speaker, that may be creating a false impression, desirable though it is to deal with these matters with the maximum of speed, because the board will have to be established, the board will have to be set up, the board will have to be mobilized, in the words of the Prime Minister, and consideration will have to be given by new members of the board, some
National Energy Board of them perhaps not familiar with these matters in the past. With the best will in the world it is bound to take some time before all these applications can be cleared up and action finally taken with regard to them. The Prime Minister's observation would give the impression that it would be pretty routine, that it will be done immediately and everything will be settled and that that is one reason why we must get this bill into operation at once. I merely want to remove the impression that this is quite as simple a procedure as the Prime Minister indicated.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
May I ask the
Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) a question? Does he not feel that the suggestion of the Prime Minister can in fact take place? Most of the detailed information has already been processed; first, by the province of Alberta; second, in the Borden commission report having regard to its limitations; and, third, by the board of transport commissioners in that it has already given some consideration to the matter with respect to one of the three applications. In view of this, does he not feel that this body of information will facilitate early consideration as suggested by the Prime Minister?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, indeed it will. There is no doubt about that. The work that has been done previously in the manner indicated by my hon. friend should facilitate the final decision of these matters. I am not suggesting anything to the contrary. I am suggesting that the impression that might have been created was that all the board would have to do would be to meet after it was established and process these export permit applications and that that could be done very quickly. I would hope it would be done as quickly as possible. But the new board is bound to look into the work done previously by other agencies concerning this matter if that board is to be as responsible as the Prime Minister said it must be in considering these matters. The Prime Minister also said as found on page 4025:
I agree that it is essential that these matters be thoroughly investigated. I am not complaining at all.
He was talking about what he said might be a delay on the part of the government of Alberta. All I am trying to point out is that, with the best will in the world, once the board is set up it will require some time to take final action with respect to these matters.
There is one other point that has a bearing on this question of what is a just and

National Energy Board reasonable price. The Prime Minister said, and I quoted this a few moments ago:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interests.
Just and reasonable as determined by a board and subject to confirmation by a government. Then he went on to make this very important statement which I think should be put on the record again and perhaps confirmed by the minister if it is to be confirmed. It is found on page 4025 at the bottom of the second column and is as follows:
With the implementation of this legislation, no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their industries-
I think that word must have been "energy".
-than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy.
In other words, the Prime Minister in those words, and I think I am being very fair to him in this interpretation, has given the assurance-on what basis I do not know-that the price paid by United States consumers of Canadian gas will not be less than that paid by Canadian consumers of Canadian gas, without any qualification or condition attached to that assurance. Perhaps the minister will deal with what I thought was a pretty rash statement on the part of the Prime Minister having regard to the conditions surrounding the export of gas the conditions of sale and the varying circumstances that enter into the pricing of gas for export.
Finally, may I mention the situation regarding section 87 having to do with oil imports and exports. It has already been dealt with in great detail and I do not propose to do so in detail at this time. Last evening the hon. member for Calgary South complained that in my earlier statement I had given no indication that I appreciated the fact that emergencies might develop with regard to oil which might require governmental action. I know that he was no doubt thinking of an emergency which would require action with regard to imports so that western oil could be moved east under certain circumstances.
My own position and the position of our party on this matter is quite clear. I have said previously and I am glad to repeat it how that the economic market for western Canadian oil is the northwestern part of the United States. In a well-ordered economic society that is where it would be going at the present time and that is where it is going although not in the quantities we hoped notwithstanding the removal of the restrictions

the other day. That is where it would be going in a well-ordered economic society. However-the Prime Minister quoted words to this effect that I have already used-if ever the policy of the United States makes it impossible for us to market our oil in the United States no Canadian government is going to let that oil remain in the ground and any Canadian government is bound to take the kind of steps which may be required to market that oil in Canada, indeed, in the east.
I am not complaining about that. I hope that will not be necessary because it is not the most desirable way of marketing that oil at the present time. If it is necessary, it will have to be done. I also add that that kind of government policy is of a very far-reaching character indeed and goes beyond the commercial in its implications, just as the building of a transcontinental railway involves something far more than a commercial venture. That kind of situation would require government action at the time perhaps with regard to the import of oil but it would be of such a far-reaching character that our complaint is that this action should be taken with the knowledge and consent of parliament.
There is no likelihood of that action being required at the present time, at least if we believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill). When the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that the case with respect to licensing imports of oil, contrasted with exports, is different and more complicated and he does not propose to argue that case fully because it would be premature to do so until the second report of the Borden commission in respect of this matter has been received and considered; if the Minister of Trade and Commerce says it is not necessary even to explain to the house why this might have to be done in the future, surely we have the duty and the right to object to a clause in the bill which gives the government that particular power which the minister himself says does not need to be argued at this time because there is no immediate emergency which might require that power. That is the burden of our complaint with regard to this particular clause and we will come back to it when we are in committee.
So far as the amendment is concerned, the official opposition will not, of course, be able to support it because it would surely be entirely inconsistent for us to support an amendment on second reading which is opposed to giving second reading to the bill itself. I know it is not possible to move an amendment on second reading to send a bill to a committee although it is possible to move an amendment that the subject matter of a

bill be sent to a committee, which is the nature of the amendment before us. The effect, however, of supporting this particular amendment would be to kill the bill and the principles involved in the bill.

speechtext:
On this main motion for second reading, Mr. Speaker- and may I say that I think I am one of those who have not spoken on the formal motion now before us-I think it would be well to attempt to summarize the impressions we have been able to get from what has been said so far in the debate, the statement of the minister and the discussion that has taken place.
