speechtext:
As I said earlier, considerable discussion has taken place over quite a number of days on this matter during which we have heard expressions of opinion by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). I imagine these are the official approaches to the problem and to the bill. We have had speeches by members of the official opposition, by members of the government party and by members of the C.C.F. party. As the motion indicates, we have come to the conclusion that it would not be in the best interests of the Canadian people, the consumers who would be supplied by gas and oil pipe lines, the orderly development of these industries or of the other types of energy which exist in Canada for us to give endorsation to the principle of the bill.
As has been indicated-and these are only general statements at the moment-this bill consolidates the provisions of other acts that are at present on the statute books dealing with the question of oil and gas pipe lines. The statutes concerning that matter are the Pipe Lines Act and the Exportation of Power

and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. The provisions of those particular acts, with the exception of one section in the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, are consolidated into this particular bill. In the consolidation in this bill now before us of these, as I suppose you could loosely call them, beneficial provisions in so far as being beneficial to the consumers and citizens of Canada are concerned, and as poor as those provisions were, we find that many of the saving features of the Pipe Lines Act and of the Exportation of Power and Fluids and the Importation of Gas Act have been watered down. We find that, generally speaking, the protective features, in so far as protecting the interests of the consumers and the citizens of Canada are concerned, are less favourable in the bill now before us than they were previously.
Coupled with the tremendous insistence on the concentration of power and authority- and I do not mean energy power such as electrical power; I mean power of individuals- to be vested in the cabinet, that is the most objectionable feature that we find in this particular piece of legislation. We are absolutely opposed, as we always have been, to the granting of dictatorial powers of this nature and to this extent to the government of this nation, whether that government is of Conservative stripe or of Liberal stripe, and irrespective of the type of political philosophy it may embrace.
There was a considerable amount of discussion in years past about the dictatorial powers of certain cabinet ministers in the former administration. Certain parties who were the champions of the rights of parliament in those days are now reversing themselves and insisting upon substantiating the same type of autocratic or authoritative control vested in the hands of 22 members of this House of Commons, so far as this particular bill is concerned. We are not vacillating in our approach to the question as did the Liberals when they condemned with all the fire they could generate and muster the provisions of the bill and complained about the insistence upon dictatorial powers being given to the cabinet, and then they turn around and indicate their support for a sort of confined or controlled lead. They must be under a misapprehension that instead of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) piloting this bill through the house it is their old friend C. D. Howe because one would certainly gather from their gleeful endorsation of its provisions which they say they abhor and do not like that the ghost of C. D. Howe must be overhanging the Liberal party and deciding what their attitude should be.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to this amendment. We have before us an amendment which will allow us to give some consideration to this bill and give an opportunity to the government to introduce the bill in a much more acceptable and honest condition. This bill which we have before us refers in the main to gas and oil, yet when we look to find what a national energy board might be expected to embrace we find this bill could cover a great many other sources of energy besides those of gas and oil. It could cover the regulation of solar energy, electrical energy, atomic energy and thermo energy,

all energy supplied from a number of sources in a number of ways. This bill has failed to take into consideration that if we are going to give to Canada a truly national energy board then we are going to have to regulate and make available under the act direction for all the various segments which go to make up the energy resources of this country.
The Liberals have pointed out that they were for many of these things. They also pointed out they were opposed to some of the major clauses of this bill. I think their position has not been justifiable with their own consciences, where you support something which you say is wrong in principle. The member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) pointed out that when the Borden commission sat on energy and made its report, 23 of the recommendations of the Borden commission were favourably considered by the government and 11 were rejected.

speechtext:
I was just trying to point out that conditions hark back to the pipe line debate of some years ago and that these conditions have set the stage for the energy bill which is before us. But this energy bill is not satisfactory in any shape or form because,

as I think it is generally agreed, the Canadian people are entitled to have a board set up which will handle our natural resources in the best and most advantageous way for the benefit of all. This bill fails to establish such a board. For example, it fails to take the coal industry into consideration, and it fails to include the atomic energy industry about which much more will be heard in the near future. It also failed to take hydroelectric power into consideration, with the exception of the export of such power.
In the climate which existed a year or two ago, when there was difficulty in raising money and when the government would not concern itself about raising funds for national development of energy resources, then, I think, this bill might have been introduced and might have received the support of some hon. members here. But today, with a government which says that it is going to develop the natural resources of northern Canada, particularly; a government which says it is going to take advantage of the natural resources that we have, and use them to the best of its ability, this measure loses a good deal of its point.
The measure needs a great deal of study, fundamentally, and I do not think we can even agree with the terms of the bill. If this bill is going to be called the national energy bill it will have to take into consideration all the forms of energy I have mentioned. This may raise difficulties for the government, and we may have to concede that it might be exceedingly difficult, because they seem to work much better in terms of experience than they do in foresight. I agree they had some success with the vision, but they should put these visionaries to work in developing many of the advantages which the Canadian people could receive from a properly designed board which would take into consideration nuclear energy. This form of energy may be a few days ahead but we are faced across all Canada with the failing of the sources of energy we have used in the past, particularly electricity generated by hydro developments. We have been faced even in the province of Ontario, which is blessed with many hydro facilities, with the possibility that within the foreseeable future, and the near foreseeable future, that hydro power will no longer be available and that there will be no future developments of that nature.
Ontario is going as far north, now, as Otter Rapids near James Bay to put in hydro developments and while there are two or three projects in this area they are limited and the end potential as we know it in that area has now been blocked out and indicated.
National Energy Board Yet we are going to be faced continually with greater need for energy and electric power in the province of Ontario, and we have given no consideration in this bill to the one large source of energy of which the Canadian, people have an abundance.
We speak sometimes of the surplus that we have of wheat and of the problems we are going to have in disposing of this surplus; wheat, but we are going to have a much, larger surplus of uranium oxide in a very short while. We are now in a position where we can see no sale or a very limited sale for uranium oxide after 1962, and I suggest that, the government might with advantage have given this board the duty to decide how our atomic energy resources should be developed in order to supply Canadian homes and industries with heat, light and power.
However, the words have never been men-, tioned. And in those parts of Canada where it is impossible to put in transmission lines for power today, an alternative solution is yet possible. We talk about the development of the far north of Canada even in the ice and snow areas. Why has the government not given some consideration in this bill to the use and development of solar energy which would not require the use of extensive transmission lines and which would allow certain developments to take place in the far north which it is very difficult to achieve at the present time? We have given no consideration to these matters and I do not see how the government can be proud of the energy bill if it has not given consideration to all the forms of energy which we have available to us in Canada.
I think there has been some small discussion over the matter of gas and oil, but I think that all we are doing is incorporating a number of bills which we already have in force. I think the machinery is already in force and that it will allow us to export all the oil and gas we wish if the government would just relax some of the restrictions which it has placed on the board they have now. The proposed board will have no restrictions. This board is going to have only advisory functions and I would suggest that maybe the civil service could through its officers probably perform the advisory functions that would be necessary and that the governor in council could, in fact, run this national energy board all by himself, and there would be no need for a board and no need for five men to advise him.
Again, we are faced in Canada with the fact that all these forms of national energy have not been taken into consideration. We have given consideration only to the western

National Energy Board members who are concerned with gas and oil. In my part of the country, too, we are interested in this new form of energy, but it no longer becomes a national form of energy -it is passed through pipe lines and it becomes the product of a number of people who are out to make a fast profit.
When it reaches northern Ontario and other areas it gives the people no advantage that they are not already getting from coal, oil and other normal sources of energy which they have had to use in the past. This natural resource has not been used to the advantage and development of secondary industries and has not been used to the advantage and development of new areas by supplying them with a new form of energy. I suggest that we do not need a national energy bill to provide the Canadian people with the development that the people were told would come about if they would allow a pipe line to be built from the west to the east to supply gas to eastern Canada. Gas has turned out to be a product that is competitive and only competitive and it offers no advantages in the field of secondary industries.
I think many of the considerations involved in the bringing of this natural energy to eastern Canada are going to have to be faced again by the Canadian people. It is rumoured at the present time that very shortly another pipe line will be built through northern Ontario from the west. One of the large contracting companies is going around telling people that they hope to be in our area again this fall and that they will be looking for crews. They are expressing the hope that the people who worked for them last year will be available this fall for the new pipe line.
If this bill were going to serve any useful purpose I suggest that a page would have to be taken out of the history of the trans-Canada pipe line and steps would have to be taken to remedy all those factors that were found not to be advantageous to the people of northern Ontario. This has not been done in the bill. There is absolutely nothing in the bill that is not already found in a number of other statutes.
I mentioned before the matter of expropriation. The government did not even write into the bill a new expropriation provision. They used the old law.

I was just pointing out that this has been a source of grievance and I would have thought that the bill before us would have taken care of it. A national


energy board is being set up to control all sources of energy in Canada and I presume it is not intended to amend the legislation next year or in a week or two. I presume that the Canadian people will have to operate for a long time under the bill as it now appears before us. I wish to suggest that some of the faults found in present acts could have and should have been remedied in this bill so as to permit the Canadian people to profit from the mistakes that have been made in the past.
Another factor that enters into the situation is the matter of making money from these new sources of energy. We have all heard about the many mistakes made in the past with regard to the financing of the trans-Canada pipe line. Let us remember that the trans-Canada pipe line was probably one of the best opportunities we have had to bring about equalization of conditions in those areas suffering from inadequacy by making available to them a source of energy at a very low cost. However, we allowed certain types of financing to take place.
The hon. member for Calgary South is an expert on gas and oil. He has been connected with this field for many years. I think he is honestly concerned with gas and oil, and I am not sure that that applies to many other people in that field. I believe he is sincerely interested in the development of gas and oil and therefore would be interested in the financial basis for organizing and operating gas companies and gas distribution lines. I was surprised when he said he did not agree that there should be a clause in the bill making provision for a fair and reasonable rate, a fair and reasonable tariff and a fair and reasonable return in connection with gas and gas distribution. That is what I understood him as saying although he indicates that that is not so. I am quite willing to accept that because I do not believe he thinks that way. I do not think that the member for Calgary South believes that. I think he believes he can exist in that industry and that the industry itself can exist for a long time only if a much more ethical and orthodox method of financing is followed.
But, Mr. Speaker, we are interested in this only as history because I do not think the Canadian people will ever allow it to happen again. When they elected this government to office they gave their answer to the mistakes the Liberals had made in this field and the Canadian people will not permit another government to do the same thing.
We are giving consideration now to the development of a national energy board but we find that there are several other sources of energy to which the government has given

no consideration at all. Are we going to wait for the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes? Are we going to wait until its use in weapons is outlawed? It will then be necessary to dispose of the uranium oxide and we will have to seek possible methods of developing energy from that source. Incidentally, Canada should be very proud of its position because we have an almost unlimited amount of uranium oxide available.
I am sure that before too long we will be faced with the establishment of plants that will use atomic energy as a cheap and reasonable source of energy, particularly in those areas where there are now no sources of energy. I am thinking particularly of the James and Hudson bay areas which we wish to develop. I presume the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources <Mr. Hamilton) has given consideration to this matter. We have a large iron ore deposit in this area and all we need is some source of energy that is readily available without terrific transportation costs. Then we will be able to reduce the iron ore into iron oxide or other forms of iron and be able to distribute these products around the world much more cheaply than shipping them to others parts of Canada and we will not have to ship the iron ore to Germany or Great Britain in order to have it processed. I suggest that both solar and atomic energy will eventually be available in these areas where transportation is difficult.

In considering this bill I was interested to listen the other day to the Prime Minister of the country. He spoke of the immense resources in Saskatchewan. There are certain developments in that province that I would have thought the Prime Minister would have been very proud of. We are very happy to have many people from Saskatchewan in northern Ontario. Some of my best friends came from that province. Some of them have always told me that John Diefenbaker was a different kind of guy; he was not really a Conservative; he was a very good guy and he was the champion of the rights of the small people of the province of Saskatchewan. When I heard him say he was very unhappy about some conditions in the province and particularly with the people who have decided on what kind of provincial government they should have and with the decisions that had been taken I was very surprised. I am going to be very happy to tell my friends that he is not the champion of the little people of Saskatchewan who made the decision a long time ago as to what kind of government they wanted. The Prime Minister mentioned several conditions there, but he pointed out that conditions are not really so bad in Saskatchewan. They have gone into certain forms of assistance in the development of new industries

of Northern Affairs and National Resources):

1.	Since January 1, 1951, have any proclamations been issued pursuant to subsection 2 of section 4 of the Indian Act?
2.	If so, what are the details of each such proclamation?
3.	Have any such proclamations been revoked?
Answer by: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
1.	Since January 1, 1951, three proclamations have been issued pursuant to subsection 2 of section 4 of the Indian Act.
2.	(a) In January 1958, section 93 (a) (i) and (b), and sections 95 and 96 of the Indian Act were made inapplicable to a parcel of land containing 162 acres, more or less, in Musqueam Indian reserve No. 2, leased to Shaughnessy heights golf club of Vancouver.
(b)	In September 1954, section 73 (2) of the Indian Act was made inapplicable to the river desert band, Maniwaki Indian agency. This proclamation provided for a reduced number of councillors and was issued at the request of the band.
(c)	In November 1953, section 73 of the Indian Act was made inapplicable to the Mohawks of the Bay of Quinte band, Tyendinaga agency. This proclamation provided for a reduced number of councillors and was issued at the request of the band.
3.	No.
